summary: This informational document gives a methodology for benchmarking the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) performance of devices, focusing on basic session setup and registration. It goes with the terminology in RFC 7501.

eli5.summary: This is the recipe for testing how fast phone-call servers are, so tests on different machines can be compared.

questions: what is the device under test
subtitle: A common recipe for measuring how many SIP sessions and registrations a device can handle without failing.

tldr.problem: SIP devices such as proxies, registrars and session border controllers can be configured in many ways, so raw performance numbers from different vendors are hard to compare.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines test topologies, setup parameters, an iterative algorithm that searches for the highest session attempt rate with zero errors, a report template and eight test cases covering session setup and registration.
tldr.outcome: Testers get a normalized way to compare the signaling capacity of SIP devices, but the RFC makes no claims about how to interpret the results.

today: RFC 7502 is an Informational document, published in April 2015, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is the methodology companion to RFC 7501.

sections.title: What Is Being Benchmarked
sections.content:
RFC 7502 gives the methodology for benchmarking the signaling performance of Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) devices. It pairs with the terminology in RFC 7501. It covers only basic session setup and registration.

The Device Under Test (DUT) is a network intermediary that supports RFC 3261 and acts as a registrar, redirect server, stateful proxy, Session Border Controller (SBC) or B2BUA. The tests look for the maximum SIP Registration Rate and SIP Session Establishment Rate the DUT can sustain over an extended period without failures.

Media streams are used only to see how they affect signaling. Measuring the media itself is out of scope. The overall aim is comparison, for example Vendor-A against Vendor-B, and the RFC makes no claims on how to interpret such results.
sections.eli5: It is a test for machines that connect phone calls. The test asks how many calls per second the machine can start before it makes a mistake.

sections.title: Test Topologies
sections.content:
In every topology a tester, called the Emulated Agent (EA), sends traffic into the DUT and absorbs traffic coming out of it. Figure 1 puts the DUT between two interfaces of the EA with any media flowing directly between the endpoints. Figure 2 has the media flowing through the DUT. Figure 3 is used for registration tests, where the EA sends requests to the DUT and reads the responses.

The RFC warns that these tests generate large volumes of data, so hubs, switches and routers in the path must be able to cope. During registration the DUT may involve backend network elements and data stores. Those affect response time, so registration and re-registration tests are kept separate and should use the same backend elements to get a stable metric.
sections.eli5: A pretend caller sits on both sides of the machine being tested. Sometimes the voices go around the machine and sometimes straight through it.

sections.title: Test Setup Parameters
sections.content:
Many choices change the results, so the RFC requires that they be reported with them. These are the SIP transport protocol (for example TCP, UDP, TLS or websockets), the connection management strategy for connection-oriented transports, the media protocol (for example RTP or SRTP), the codec, the session duration and the session attempt rate.

Connection management matters because for transports such as TLS the cryptographic handshake happens every time a connection is opened. For media, a voice test uses a single media stream and a voice and video test uses two.

Session Duration is set in seconds. A value of 0 means the EA sends a BYE immediately after it receives a 200 OK to the INVITE. A value longer than the test means a BYE is never sent. For the session tests, the EA is configured to send the final 2xx-class response as quickly as it can, with no added delay.

Section 5 supplies a report template. It records the settings above plus total sessions attempted, media packet size, establishment threshold time, the TLS ciphersuite and the IPsec profile, followed by the resulting Session Establishment Rate, Registration Rate and Re-registration Rate.
sections.eli5: Before comparing two races you must write down the track, the weather and the shoes. Here you write down the settings so nobody can say the test was unfair.

sections.title: The Benchmarking Algorithm
sections.content:
All test cases use one algorithm. Its goal is to find the largest session attempt rate R, in sessions per second, that the DUT handles with zero errors while N sessions are attempted. The RFC's pseudocode sets N to 50000 and starts the rate r at 100 (the tester may pick another value, or use a number supplied by the vendor).

Each round sends N sessions at rate r. If all succeed, the rate is raised by a weight w, initially 0.10. If some fail, the rate is lowered by a decrease weight d, and both weights are adjusted but never drop below 0.10. The loop ends when the rate has stopped improving for 10 rounds, and the highest rate reached is reported as R. A simulation in the R language is in Appendix A.

The pseudocode notes that if w is small and r is 9 or less, the algorithm will not converge, because it uses floor() to adjust the rate. Start with the defaults, w of 0.10 and r of at least 100.
sections.eli5: Imagine turning up a tap until the bucket just starts to overflow. You speed up while things go well and slow down when they spill, until you find the fastest speed with no spills.

sections.title: The Test Cases
sections.content:
Eight test cases each state an objective, a procedure and expected results. Case 6.1 is a baseline with no DUT present, which can be used to normalize results from different testbeds. Cases 6.2 to 6.4 measure session establishment without media, with media that bypasses the DUT, and with media running through the DUT. Cases 6.5 and 6.6 repeat the measurement with TLS and IPsec encryption.

Results with media that does not pass through the DUT are expected to match results without media. With media on the DUT they may be lower, depending on factors such as relaying versus transcoding, the type of media and the codec, though there may be no impact if the DUT has dedicated media-path hardware. TLS and IPsec results may be lower than plaintext SIP.

Case 6.7 measures registration rate. The registration timeout is set to at least 3600 seconds and each request goes to a distinct Address of Record. Case 6.8 re-registers the same addresses after at least 5 minutes but no more than 10 minutes, so the registrations have not yet expired, and compares the rate against case 6.7.
sections.eli5: There are several mini-races: with no helper, with a helper carrying the voices, with secret codes turned on, and with signing in many people. Each one finds the top speed in its own way.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says documents of this type do not directly affect the security of the Internet or corporate networks, as long as benchmarking is not performed on devices or systems connected to production networks. The tests are meant for a lab environment.

For security threats and countermeasures in SIP and the media layer, it points to RFC 3261, RFC 3550 and RFC 3711, among other documents.
sections.eli5: Do these tests in a practice room, not on the real network people are using, and no one gets hurt.
